reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Spina bifida is a congenital neural tube defect ranging from the hidden spina bifida occulta to the severe open myelomeningocele
Myelomeningocele exposes neural tissue and typically causes lower limb weakness, sensory loss, and bladder and bowel dysfunction whose level reflects the anatomical lesion
It is frequently associated with a Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus, which often needs cerebrospinal fluid diversion
Spina bifida occulta is usually asymptomatic and found incidentally, but cutaneous markers such as a tuft of hair, dimple, or lipoma over the spine can signal an underlying tethered cord
Periconceptional folic acid supplementation substantially reduces the risk of neural tube defects and is a key public health measure
Antenatal diagnosis is supported by maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and detailed ultrasound, allowing planning of delivery and early surgery
Early surgical closure of an open defect protects exposed neural tissue and reduces infection risk, and fetal repair is offered in selected cases
Lifelong multidisciplinary care addresses mobility, urological, orthopaedic, and neurosurgical needs including shunt surveillance and tethered cord
reference.pathophysiology: Spina bifida results from failure of the neural tube to close completely during early embryonic development, leaving a midline defect in the vertebral arches and, in open forms, in the overlying tissues. In myelomeningocele the meninges and dysplastic spinal cord protrude through the defect, so neural function below the lesion is impaired. Disordered cerebrospinal fluid dynamics and the commonly associated Chiari II malformation predispose to hydrocephalus. In occult forms the cord may be abnormally low and tethered by a thickened filum or lipoma, and growth-related traction can produce progressive neurological, urological, or orthopaedic deterioration.
additionalDifferentials: Sacrococcygeal teratoma or other congenital masses
Tethered cord syndrome from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Antenatal ultrasound and maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein for prenatal detection
MRI of the spine and brain to define the lesion, cord tethering, and associated Chiari II malformation
Cranial imaging and head circumference monitoring to detect hydrocephalus
Urodynamic and renal tract assessment for neurogenic bladder
Orthopaedic evaluation of the spine, hips, and lower limbs
redFlags: Open defect with exposed neural tissue at risk of infection needing urgent protection and closure
Signs of associated hydrocephalus or Chiari II brainstem dysfunction in an infant
New or progressive neurological, urological, or orthopaedic decline suggesting tethered cord or shunt failure
Fever or CSF leak indicating possible meningitis or ventriculitis
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies widely with the level and severity of the lesion; occulta is usually benign, whereas myelomeningocele typically causes lasting motor, sensory, and sphincter deficits, though multidisciplinary care and timely surgery improve function and reduce complications.
pitfalls: Dismissing cutaneous spinal markers that may indicate occult dysraphism and a tethered cord
Failing to monitor for evolving hydrocephalus or shunt malfunction
Overlooking neurogenic bladder and the associated risk to the upper urinary tract
Attributing new deficits in a growing child to the original lesion rather than a tethered cord
management: Early surgical closure of the myelomeningocele defect, or antenatal foetal repair in selected cases, to protect exposed neural tissue and reduce infection
Cerebrospinal fluid diversion by ventriculoperitoneal shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy for associated hydrocephalus
Neurogenic bladder management with intermittent catheterisation, anticholinergics and regular renal-tract surveillance to protect the kidneys
Structured bowel management programme for neurogenic bowel dysfunction
Orthopaedic and physiotherapy care for lower-limb weakness, spinal deformity and hip problems, with appropriate mobility aids and pressure-area skin care
Untethering surgery for a symptomatic tethered cord causing progressive neurological, urological or orthopaedic decline
Multidisciplinary follow-up, with periconceptional folic acid supplementation to prevent recurrence and genetic counselling for the family
